tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_session
tools.description: Create a new Claude Code Remote session. Returns the new session's ID and status. If environment_id is omitted, the new session inherits the calling session's environment. Combine with send_message for fan-out orchestration: spawn a sibling and send it a task. Where enabled, this session receives a <child-session-event> turn if the new session's turn fails or its worker restarts and drops background tasks; a session that finishes cleanly does not report back, so check on it with get_session (status_bucket reads 'failed' for a turn that errored, where status alone reads 'idle' either way) and list_events.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_session
schema.description: Create a new Claude Code Remote session. Returns the new session's ID and status. If environment_id is omitted, the new session inherits the calling session's environment. Combine with send_message for fan-out orchestration: spawn a sibling and send it a task. Where enabled, this session receives a <child-session-event> turn if the new session's turn fails or its worker restarts and drops background tasks; a session that finishes cleanly does not report back, so check on it with get_session (status_bucket reads 'failed' for a turn that errored, where status alone reads 'idle' either way) and list_events.

append_system_prompt.description: Text appended to the new session's system prompt.

blob_limit_kb.description: Optional. Files larger than this many KB are left out of the checkout; git fetches one on demand when a command reads it. Requires source_url. Set it for very large repositories, whose sessions otherwise fail to start for lack of disk space. Ignored when sparse_checkout_paths is set.

clone_depth.description: Optional number of commits of history to fetch (default 50). Requires source_url. Lower it for very large repositories.

environment_id.description: Environment ID — a tagged ID starting with 'env_' (or 'ccpool_' for self-hosted pools). Defaults to the calling session's environment. Do NOT invent a value — call list_environments to get the user's real environment_ids. When this resolves to the remote_cowork environment (explicitly or via inheritance), a Claude Cowork session is spawned — the account's enabled skills, plugins and the Cowork system prompt are assembled server-side, and only prompt, title, model and tags are read (source_url, extra_allowed_tools, append_system_prompt and environment_variables are ignored so the caller cannot widen the tool surface).

extra_allowed_tools.description: Extra tool names pre-approved without a user permission prompt. Entries the calling session does not itself have pre-approved are dropped — the child never carries a grant its parent lacks.

model.description: Model ID for the new session. Defaults to the calling session's model.

outcome_branch.description: Optional branch name to push changes to. When set, the session pushes directly to this branch (no session-derived suffix appended).

permission_mode.description: Initial permission mode for the new session. Cannot be more permissive than the calling session's mode; omit to inherit it. 'plan' makes the agent propose a plan and then BLOCKS waiting for human approval via the claude.ai/code web UI — do NOT use 'plan' for autonomous child sessions that no human is watching, as they will stall indefinitely at the approval prompt.

prompt.description: Optional initial message to send to the new session.

source_revision.description: Optional git branch, tag, or commit to check out. Requires source_url. Defaults to the repo's default branch.

source_url.description: Optional git repository URL to check out.

sparse_checkout_paths.description: Optional directories, relative to the repository root. The checkout holds only these, plus the files directly in their parent folders and at the root. Requires source_url. Set it to work in part of a very large repository.

tags.description: Free-form tags to categorize the session (e.g. ["remote-agents-project:frontend"]). Editable later via set_session_tags.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_trigger
tools.description: Create a Routine (scheduled trigger). Three targeting modes: (1) default — fires into THIS SESSION, resuming the same conversation each time; (2) persistent_session_id set — fires into a SPECIFIC OTHER SESSION you name (must be in your account); (3) create_new_session_on_fire=true — spawns a FRESH SESSION in this environment on each firing. Use mode 1 for recurring work you want to pick back up yourself; mode 2 for waking a sibling session you created; mode 3 when each firing should start from a clean slate. If the result warns that the Routine stores no connectors, say so plainly when you confirm the Routine to the user and pass on the remedy it names; never report such a Routine as simply created.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_trigger
schema.description: Create a Routine (scheduled trigger). Three targeting modes: (1) default — fires into THIS SESSION, resuming the same conversation each time; (2) persistent_session_id set — fires into a SPECIFIC OTHER SESSION you name (must be in your account); (3) create_new_session_on_fire=true — spawns a FRESH SESSION in this environment on each firing. Use mode 1 for recurring work you want to pick back up yourself; mode 2 for waking a sibling session you created; mode 3 when each firing should start from a clean slate. If the result warns that the Routine stores no connectors, say so plainly when you confirm the Routine to the user and pass on the remedy it names; never report such a Routine as simply created.

connectors.description: Optional list of connector names the Routine's fired sessions may use, e.g. ["Gmail", "linear"]. Pass ONLY connectors the user explicitly asked this Routine to use — the stored grant applies to every future firing. Names resolve against the user's connected claude.ai connectors; when calling from inside a CCR session the list is further limited to connectors that session itself holds (it can only narrow that set, never widen it). Any name that cannot be resolved fails the call. Pass [] to store no connectors. Omit to keep the default behavior for this surface. The grant attaches the connectors only — individual tool calls from fired sessions still go through runtime permission checks.

create_new_session_on_fire.description: If true, each firing creates a fresh session in the calling session's environment instead of resuming an existing one. Default false. Mutually exclusive with persistent_session_id.

cron_expression.description: Standard 5-field cron expression (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week). Fields without a prefix are UTC. If you know the user's time zone, write the fields in their local time after CRON_TZ=<IANA time zone> and a space (weekdays at 8:52am in Los Angeles: CRON_TZ=America/Los_Angeles 52 8 * * 1-5). If not, ask. Minimum interval is normally hourly (some projects allow shorter); a too-frequent schedule is rejected and the error names the minimum. For hourly or every-N-hours schedules, use minute 0 (e.g. '0 * * * *', '0 */4 * * *'): the server anchors it to the creation minute ('hourly starting now'), so Routines spread across the hour instead of all firing at :00. All other schedules are stored verbatim. When a recurring schedule (run_once_at is unset) at a fixed time of day would land on the hour or half hour (a plain '9am' or '9:30'), prefer using a jittered minute value instead. Most schedules run on minute 0, so runs scheduled at those times can be delayed due to server traffic. By default, move the time 1 to 15 minutes earlier (for '9am', 8:45 to 8:59); use the number of letters in the task's name, modulo 15, plus 1. Leave midnight, a time on any other minute (e.g. 9:10) and a run that must follow an event as asked. Mutually exclusive with run_once_at. Omit both for a poke-only Routine that never fires on its own schedule.

environment_id.description: Environment ID — a tagged ID starting with 'env_' (or 'ccpool_' for self-hosted pools). Defaults to the calling session's environment. Required when calling from outside a CCR session (no session context to inherit from). Do NOT invent a value — call list_environments to get the user's real environment_ids.

initiation.description: Who wanted this: human_request — a person asked you to set this up now; human_schedule — a schedule a person set (e.g. an earlier firing) told you to; own_followup — your own check-in or follow-up on work you are already doing; own_initiative — you decided on your own that this should exist.

notifications.description: Completion notifications for this Routine. push sends to the owner's phone when a run finishes with something noteworthy; email sends the same summary to their inbox. If omitted, the setting stays unset and the server default applies at fire time. Passing this sets an explicit per-Routine choice, so list every channel you want on ({push:true, email:true} for both; {email:true} alone means email-only, push off). Pass {} to opt out of all channels. Only fresh-session-per-fire Routines (create_new_session_on_fire=true) take this; the server rejects it for self-bind or persistent_session_id Routines.

persistent_session_id.description: Optional session ID to fire into instead of this one. Must belong to the same account — the server rejects sessions you don't own. Omit to fire into this session (default). Mutually exclusive with create_new_session_on_fire.

prompt.description: The message the Routine sends on each firing. When binding to an existing session (modes 1-2), write it assuming past context — the conversation continues. In fresh-session mode (mode 3), write it as a complete standalone instruction since each firing starts from nothing.

run_once_at.description: RFC3339 timestamp for a one-shot fire (e.g. 2026-04-20T17:00:00Z). Must be in the future. Mutually exclusive with cron_expression — set one or the other, not both. After the one-shot fires the Routine disables itself with ended_reason=run_once_fired. Use exactly the time asked: the guidance on recurring schedules does not apply to a one-time run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__delete_trigger
tools.description: Delete a Routine (scheduled trigger). The Routine must belong to the calling session's account — deleting another account's Routine fails with not-found. Use this to undo a create_trigger call or to clean up Routines whose work is done. Deleting a Routine also deletes every session it started, so a session the Routine started cannot delete it. From such a session, stop the Routine with update_trigger (enabled=false) instead. A bad cron or wrong prompt does not need deletion — update_trigger fixes those in place, keeping the Routine's run history. On success, the result usually echoes the deleted Routine's last state (including its name) in the response's trigger field — callers without stored-data read access get a plain-text confirmation instead. Either way the Routine no longer exists once this returns.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__get_session
tools.description: Get details for a specific Claude Code Remote session by ID. Returns the session's title, status, status_bucket (working / blocked / review_ready / completed / failed — 'failed' means its last turn errored), creation time, and context. Every returned session carries three model fields: configured_model is the model stored at creation, echoed as stored (it may be an alias or carry a context-window suffix, so normalize before comparing); session_context.model is the model the session is currently set to run (the creation-time model, or a later switch or refusal fallback); external_metadata.last_served_model is the model the CLI ran the latest turn on, which also reflects turn-scoped fallbacks (overload or unavailable) that do not change session_context.model. To detect a switch or fallback in a child session, compare configured_model against both session_context.model and external_metadata.last_served_model; the fallback notices in list_events give the reason. Omit session_id to describe this session.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__list_triggers
tools.description: List Routines (scheduled triggers) owned by this account. Use it to find trigger IDs (trig_...) for update_trigger and delete_trigger. From a thread in a Slack channel, only Routines that fire into that thread's session are listed unless all_in_channel is true. Each entry has the Routine's id, name, cron_expression, run_once_at, enabled state, ended_reason, next_run_at, created_at, persistent_session_id, and last_run. last_run is the most recent recorded run {status, fired_at, finished_at, session_id}. It is absent when no run was recorded (e.g. never fired). For a Routine that wakes an existing session, last_run records that the wake was delivered (SUCCEEDED) or failed to deliver, not how the turn went, unless run tracking covers that session. A FAILED or repeatedly non-SUCCEEDED last_run means the Routine is not doing its job. ended_reason says why a disabled Routine is permanently disabled. suspension_reason (e.g. subscription_paused) marks a temporary hold that lifts when the owner's subscription resumes. Both empty means user-paused. One-shot Routines that already fired (e.g. delivered send_later reminders) and Routines moved to a project are hidden unless include_completed is true. Scheduled tasks stored locally by the Cowork desktop app are not listed.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__read_documentation
tools.description: The documentation for the machine and product this session runs in: a claude.ai cloud container and the settings around it (GitHub access, connectors, the environment's secrets, network access, setup script and installed tools, the session's limits, Remote Control). Read it whenever something about your container or environment comes up, whether it blocked you, you worked around it, or the person asked how to set it up. For example: the repository the work is about is not in your container, a clone or push is refused, a service you need has no connected connector, an outbound host is denied, a command-line tool is missing, you need an API key. Read it rather than answering from memory because these settings move and get renamed faster than your training data, and a page says what is true now: the current steps, where in the product the person makes the change, and what you can do yourself. Reading a page also helps the person directly: in the Claude Code app they see a card with a button that takes them to that settings page, so they can fix it themselves while you carry on. Call it with no topic to list the pages and when each applies; call it with a topic to read that page. Read a page each time a different topic comes up; one read per topic is enough. It is read-only and needs no approval. It has nothing on bugs in the code you are working on.

This is a thin wrapper over create_trigger (a self-bind + run_once_at Routine); the returned trigger_id can be passed to delete_trigger to cancel before it fires, and the Routine disables itself after firing once.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

A `trait G[\X\] extends {S, T}` whose only extender is `object H extends {G[\ZZ32\], V}` meets 7C's rule for both clauses; every value of `G[\ZZ32\]` is a `V`, but `G[\ZZ32\]` is a subtype of `S` and `T` and not of `V`, and a call `f(g)` with `g : G[\ZZ32\]` has `f(S)` and `f(T)` applicable by its static type and `f(V)` not. The rule for abstract function declarations asks for "a definition for every immediate subtype" of a closed trait (`Specification/basic/functions.tex:413-415`; a team note, `Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:428-434`, "all its immediate subtraits"), where under 7C's reading the immediate subtypes and the listed types can differ (`AnyIntegral` and `Integral`) | OPEN (for Pavol) | specification gap | `Specification/basic/traits.tex:235-252`; `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:583-604`; `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:275-307`; `Specification/basic/functions.tex:370-415`; the team's future-work item "We agreed to revise the Meet rule to address this with the coverage check" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:269-285`) | `compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/probes/between/BetweenTwoClosed.fss` with `BetweenTwoClosed.txt` (on the base the compiled checker refuses `G`, "S has a comprises clause but its immediate subtype G is not eligible to extend it", and the same for `T`; walk refuses `f(S)` beside `f(T)` first, row 492); `compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/probes/skeptic/SkBetweenAssign.fss` with `SkBetweenAssign.txt`, and `probes/skeptic/between-narrow.txt` (the rung's skeptic, under a shadow of rung Y's rule); `compile-ladder/climb-batch-7C/merged-tests/between-y.txt` (the gather, with rung Y's landed checker) | ours (climb batch 7C, rung X, 2026-09-28) | Home 3: neither the decision (POSITIONS 2026-09-28, `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause) nor rung Y's section settles the new text of these passages, and the rung reports them without choosing (its batch record's stop); the Appendix I entry says they are not revised and their question is not settled (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1311-1316`). == explorations/reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md:26-101

### 1.6 Item 30: a generic declaration beside a plain one at run time (D28)

- The paper contradicts the default and gives the rule. The record chose "the instance the value fixes, the least instance where it fixes none", Welterweight's rule (`Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:189-192`: "l_j is the type inferred for P_j", the lower bound), and recorded Naden's return-type restriction as future work, weighing Naden's 2012 objection that programmers could not follow execution without static types (`literature.md` § 1). The paper, with Steele among its authors, took the other road: static return types are carried to run time ([R-Method], lines 888-896), and the instance is the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound and the static return type's constraint, never the lower bound alone (lines 1274-1284). It says in so many words that the lower-bound rule could not be proven.
- Where the two rules agree: a parameter fixed by an invariant position in a parameter type (`grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])`), since lower and upper bound coincide, which is the case the judgement's example and rung W's row 157 concern. Where they differ: a parameter that is the whole type of a parameter or occurs only covariantly. `id[\T\](x: T): Box[\T\]` called through `r: Any = id(z)` with a `ZZ32` value gives `Box[\ZZ32\]` under the record's rule and `Box[\Any\]` under the paper's; a later dispatch on the box tells them apart.
- Where they meet answer 8: the revival's static promotion instantiates `op[\T extends Number\](z, w)` at `ZZ64` and annotates the call's result `ZZ64`; the paper's run-time rule then gives `Number ⊓ ZZ64 = ZZ64`, the same instance. So the paper's rule reproduces rung I's static choice at run time from the annotation, which the "least instance" rule does not promise.
- Walk cannot apply the paper's rule: it has no static types, so no static return type to constrain the instance; the value's type is all it has. That is walk's limit, as for coercion (judgement, item 7).
- Do differently, in batch 7b: rung S states the paper's rule as the designers' latest word in the dispatch paragraph (the dispatched declaration's parameters instantiated at the intersection of their upper bounds under the call's static return type, never `Bottom`), and states in a callout that both implementations today take the value's type where nothing fixes the parameter, walk by necessity and the compiled path until phase 5. Rung C adds one expected-failure pair for the case where the two rules differ (the `Box[\Any\]` shape above) beside the two it already adds. Rung W's row-157 fix stays, being walk's best. Phase 5's list gains one line: the dispatcher needs the call's static return type, which the team's code generator does not pass (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:2048`, "Not sure what to do with return type"). Cost: wording in a rung that already edits the passage, one test pair, one plan line.

### 1.7 The implicit bound `Any` (Q1; the judgement's item 3)

- The paper confirms it: "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (lines 418-419). The judgement's item 3 stands with this as its deciding citation; rung S cites it in the callout that revises `trait-parameters.tex:49-50`. Nothing else changes.

### 1.8 Row 447, the written `extends Object` bound, and every `Bottom` binding (D23 decision 2; the judgement's commission error 1 and item 2)

- The paper contradicts the mechanism and gives the fix. Its type system "requires that both static and dynamic type inference algorithms instantiate type parameters with non-Bottom types" (lines 845-847, 884, 1119-1120), the solving step "never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom" (lines 1005-1006), and an otherwise unconstrained parameter takes the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound, `Any` by default, and the static return type's constraint.
- Under that rule the crashes of row 447 do not arise. `fail[\T\]("...")` in a `ZZ32` value position is instantiated at `ZZ32`; `r: Any = et(z)` instantiates `et` at `Any`, and `BoxT[\Any\]` is a class that exists, where `BoxT[\Bottom\]` carried as `java/lang/Object` was not. The compiled checker's solver does the opposite today: an inference variable left open is bound to `BOTTOM` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1954-1955`, `killIvars`; `Formula.scala:524`), which is why rung B's written bound "works" and why the kept expected type of rung I still binds `Bottom` (row 447's later notes). The Working Draft's own note asks "Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers BottomTypes for static parameters?" (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:233-234`); the paper is the designers' answer.

### 1. The rule

**Decided: way 2**, reading A of `option-2-soundness.md`: the coercion chapter's order over declarations, with applicability and specificity taken on declared, quantified domains as answer 9 words them, and answer 8's promotion as the instantiation of the selected declaration, its coercions inserted statically and the rewritten call dispatching on the converted values.

**Stated for the specification** (rung T's inference chapter; batch 7b's rung S for the coercion chapter's cross-reference):

> *Resolution* (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:472-476`, `:533-553`, unchanged in substance). For a static call `f(A)` or `A₀.f(A)`, let Σ be the declarations of `f` applicable to the call without coercion, a declaration with static parameters being applicable when some instance within its bounds is (`Papers/Types/setup.tick:393-397`; answer 9), and compared on those quantified domains. If Σ is not empty, its most specific declaration is selected. Otherwise, among the declarations applicable with coercion, the one whose parameter type is no less specific (`⪯`, `:486-513`) than every other's is selected; the overloading rules guarantee that it exists and is unique, and where they do not, the call is a static error.
>
> *Instantiation* (the inference chapter). The static arguments of the selected declaration are then inferred: a static parameter takes the narrowest type, under `⪯`, that every argument constraining it is substitutable for (`:417-432`), its bounds permitting; for number arguments this is the narrowest type every one of them converts into (answer 8). The coercions this instance needs are inserted into the call statically, like any coercion resolved statically (`:584-591`).
>
> *Dispatch* (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:262-276`). The rewritten call dispatches at run time, by subtyping and without further coercion, to the most specific declaration applicable to the converted values.
>
> *Numerals* (Q1; decision 4 below). Where a numeral's candidate types are incomparable under `⪯`, in either step, the numeral is read as `ZZ32`, or as `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit.

**Reasons.**
- One principle at two levels, not two rules. A conversion makes a call possible and never changes which body runs when a body already fits (`conversions-coercions.tex:279-282`, `:472-476`). Answer 8 chooses among instances of one body; it never chooses between bodies. So the designers' order and answer 8 do not conflict once applicability is read on declared domains, which answer 9 already decided (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md` section 3.4: "inference instantiates the chosen declaration; it does not precede the comparison").
- Sound, with one sentence. `option-2-soundness.md` section 1: the Meet Rule, the uniqueness facts and the appendix lemma speak of declared domains, which reading A does not change (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:247-274`, `:449-470`; `Specification/appendices/overloading-coercion.tex:75-96`). Section 2: the converted call's re-dispatch to `plain64` is type-safe by the return-type rule over every instance (measured, `O2Z64` on the rule and opt2 builds). Section 3: the Meet Rule does its job (`O2Meet`, every build). Section 4: it is answer 9's own order.
- The designers' record is unanimous for this order, and the type group's later word does not contradict it. The coercion chapter (2007-2009; `0f49d8698`). The checker's coercion-first ranking (Hilburn, 2009-08-18, `fc99e1ef2`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1085-1095`, opened and read). The compiled library, whose `=` and `=/=` are per type with no arm over `Any` or `Number` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:123-124`, `:167-168`, `:229-230`, `:299-300`, `:359-360`, `:412-413`, `:445`), general equality being `Equality[\T\] comprises T` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi:24-26`), so that under this order `z = 0` reaches `ZZ32`'s own `=` with the numeral converted: by reading, Σ is empty, and `(ZZ32, ZZ32) ⪯ (ZZ64, ZZ64)` and `⪯ (ZZ, ZZ)` because `IntLiteral`, the one type that converts into `ZZ32`, excludes both (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390`). The 2011 paper and Welterweight have no coercion (`Papers/Types/rules.tick:118-129`; `Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:67`, `:187-193`). Protocol principle 1 and POSITIONS 2026-09-23 give the later word more weight where the two conflict; here nothing conflicts.
- The peers. Java (strict invocation before loose), C++ (an exact match beats a promotion beats a conversion, and a user-defined conversion ranks lowest), Swift (a score that counts conversions first) and Julia (never converts in dispatch; the library's catch-alls promote) all put an unconverted arm first; C# alone ranks by the conversion's target (`conversion-overloading-ways.md` section 6). Pavol asked for the rule "from type theory and the peers' implementations"; the peers' majority is the designers' order.
- Speed. Under this order no call converts when an arm fits; a conversion is a run-time allocation (`option-2-soundness.md` section 6, `coerce_ZZ64(FZZ32)` per call). The fast path is the library's arm at the exact type, which the compiled library's design reaches on every call. On the fork itself the stamped instance is taken, with no dispatch test (`option-2-soundness/captures/javap-O2Explicit.txt`).
- What Pavol's idea becomes, and why it is not taken. Way 4 is its sound form (`conversion-overloading-ways.md` sections 8 and 9, way 4): "specific" read as the chapter's `⪯`, a candidate taken only when it is `⪯` every other, the designers' order as the fallback; unique by antisymmetry (`conversions-coercions.tex:503-509`). Not adopted because: (i) it ranks a conversion as free, adding one per call wherever a converted arm outranks an unconverted one; (ii) most specific is not fastest, `z1 =/= z2` reaching `QQ`'s `=/=` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:71`, `:406`; by reading); (iii) it reverses `:472-476` for plain arms (`p(NarrowOf(1))` to `p(Wide)`, `ProjectFortress/tests/CoercionOverloadRungC.fss:45` and `compiler_tests/XXXCoercionAnyOverloadRungC.fss`; `ee(5)` refused by rung R's rule under answer 12); (iv) its walk half decides from run-time types and needs a further condition where a program's own conversion goes into a trait excluding the static type (the ways note, way 4's soundness paragraph); (v) it reaches shapes no library or microGPT declaration has (`before-n-questions.md` A.3; `PROBE-K.md:11`, `:17`), at the price of a probe, phase 5's defect 3 pulled forward (`O2Excl` under opt2), the proof appendix rescoped, and tens of lines in the checker and in walk's per-call dispatch, which caches nothing for an overloaded method. C# is one peer; the designers are unanimous. Way 4 is recorded here as the way back if a future library shape needs it, priced as above.
- The other ways. Way 1 (batch N as the shadows built it) is unsound: applicability is not closed downward, so the specification's promise that the run-time choice is at least as specific fails (`O2Wide`, `option-2-soundness.md` section 2; `advanced/overloading.tex:466-468`). Way 3 is unsound as it stands (`O2Tie`). Ways 5 and 6 add refusals or a second relation. Way 7 reverses part of answer 8. Way 8 refuses calls the specification promises an arm. \section{Coercion Resolution}
\seclabel{resolving-coercion}
For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a
declaration that is applicable without coercion.  If so, the most
specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are
explicitly added to the functional call.  If more than one coercion is
possible then the coercion that yields the most specific type is
chosen.  \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} describe overloading rules for the
declarations of coercions and overloaded functionals that guarantee
there exists always a most specific coercion when two or more are possible.
A declaration with static parameters is applicable, without or with coercion,
when some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their bounds is, and
declarations are compared on the parameter types they declare
(\secref{functional-applicability}, \secref{resolving-overloading}); the
declaration selected is then instantiated as \secref{static-arg-inference}
describes, with the rule for a numeral whose conversions tie
(\secref{numeral-default}).
\revision{revival-overloading}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not say
here when a declaration with static parameters is applicable.
The revival decided on 28~September 2026 that a coercion makes a call possible
and never changes which declaration runs when one is applicable without it:
declarations are chosen in the order this section gives, on the parameter types
they declare, and the declaration chosen is then instantiated.}

We first define a notion of more specific types in the presence of coercion.
Recall from \secref{type-relations} that Fortress defines an
\emph{exclusion} relation between types which is denoted by $\excludes$.

For types $T$ and $U$, we say that $T$ \emph{rejects} $U$,
and write $T \rejects U$, if for all coercions to $T$, the type coerced
from excludes $U$:
\[
T \rejects U \iff \forall A: A \coercedefto T \implies A \excludes U.
\]
Note that $T \rejects U$ implies $U \not\coercesto T$.

We say that $T$ is \emph{no less specific} than $U$, and write $T
\morespecificeq U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ excludes, can be
coerced to, and rejects $U$:
\[
T \morespecificeq U \iff
T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor
(T \excludes U \logicand T \coercesto U \logicand T \rejects U).
\]

The $\morespecificeq$ relation is reflexive and antisymmetric but not
necessarily transitive.  It is possible, for example, for
three types, $T$, $U$ and $V$, each excluding the other two,
to have coercions from $T$ to $U$ and from $U$ to $V$.  In
this case, $T \morespecificeq U$ and $U \morespecificeq V$ but
$T \not\morespecificeq V$.

Notice that if two tuple types have a bijective correspondence
between their element types then the $\morespecificeq$ relationship between
the tuple types is equivalent to applying the $\morespecificeq$
relation elementwise.

We say that $T$ is \emph{more specific} than $U$, and write $T
\morespecific U$, if $T \morespecificeq U \logicand T \neq U$.

We extend the definitions of no less specific and more specific to
declarations.  We say that a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecificeq \Qs$.
Similarly, we say that a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
specific} than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps)
\morespecificeq (\Qs_0, \Qs)$.  A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more
specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$.
Similarly, a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than
a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps) \morespecific (\Qs_0,
\Qs)$.

Now we describe how to determine which coercion is applied to a given
call in terms of rewriting functional calls.  The rewriting is
for pedagogical purposes; implementation techniques may vary.

Consider a static call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$.  Let $\Sigma$ be
the set of parameter types of functional declarations of $\f$ that are
applicable to the call.
Let $\Sigma'$ be the set of parameter types of
functional declarations of $\f$ that are
applicable with coercion to the call.
If $\Sigma$ is not empty then we use the overloading resolution
described in \secref{resolving-overloading} to determine which
element of $\Sigma$ is called.
The parameter type of a declaration with static parameters is in $\Sigma$, or
in $\Sigma'$, when some instance of the declaration whose static arguments
satisfy their bounds is applicable to the call, without or with coercion; the
static arguments of the declaration selected are inferred afterwards
(\secref{static-arg-inference}).
\revision{revival-overloading}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not say
when the parameter type of a declaration with static parameters is in these
sets.}
If $\Sigma$ is empty but $\Sigma'$ is not, then we rewrite the call as
follows.  Define: \[\mathpzc{C} = \{T \in \Sigma' \mid S \coercedefto T
\logicand \As \Ovrsubtype S\}.\] Let $T \in \mathpzc{C}$ be the most
specific element of $\mathpzc{C}$.  In other words, there does not exist
$T' \in \mathpzc{C}$ such that $T' \morespecific T$.  The restrictions
given in \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} guarantee that such a $T$
exists and that it is unique.  The call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$ is
rewritten to \EXP{f(\mathrm{coercion}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(\TYP{A}))} or
\EXP{A_{0}.f(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(A))}
and the declaration with parameter
type $T$ is applied to the call.

As an example, consider the following definitions:
%trait ZZ32 excludes { ZZ64, ZZ128 } end
%trait ZZ64 excludes { ZZ128 }
%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
%end
%trait ZZ128
%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
%  coerce(z:ZZ64) = ...
%end
%
%f(z:ZZ64) = 1
%f(z:ZZ128) = 2
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}32 \KWD{excludes} \{\,\mathbb{Z}64, \mathbb{Z}128\,\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}64 \KWD{excludes} \{\,\mathbb{Z}128\,\}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}128\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\\
\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = 1\)\\
\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}128) = 2\)
\end{Fortress}
Then the call \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}32)} resolves to the
declaration \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}64)} because $\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
\morespecific \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}$, which follows from the facts that
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} excludes \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}, coerces to it, and rejects it:
the one type that coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, excludes
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.
The same facts make the two declarations of \VAR{f} a valid overloading, and the
exclusion of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} by \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} does the same for the two
coercions to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128} (\secref{more-specific-rule}).
\revision{revival-coercion-example}{The Working Draft of February 2011 declared the
three traits with no \KWD{excludes} clause and said that the resolution follows
from the fact that \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.
By the definition above, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} is then not more specific than
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}, and neither the two declarations of \VAR{f} nor the two
coercions to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128} are a valid overloading; both implementations
of the revival refuse the example as the Working Draft wrote it.
The clauses added are spelled as \library\ spell those of their integer types,
each trait excluding the wider ones.}

Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is
statically chosen for a call, this coercion is conceptually inserted
into the call.
This means that the statically chosen coercion is applied at run time.
The coercions that the instance of a declaration with static parameters needs
are chosen and inserted into the call in the same way
(\secref{static-arg-inference}).
\revision{revival-overloading}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not say
how the coercions of an instance of a declaration with static parameters are
chosen.}

For example, in the following program:
%trait A
%  coerce(c:C) = ...
%end
%trait B excludes A end
%trait C end
%object D extends {B,C} end
%
%f(a:A) = 3
%f(b:B) = 4
%
%c : C = D
%f(c)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} A\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(c\COLONOP{}C) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} B \KWD{excludes} A \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object} D \KWD{extends} \{B,C\} \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(f(a\COLONOP{}A) = 3\)\\
\(f(b\COLONOP{}B) = 4\)\\[4pt]
\(c \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} C = D\)\\
\(f(c)\)
\end{Fortress}
the call to \EXP{f(C)} resolves to the declaration
%\EXP{f(a\COLONOP{}A)}
\EXP{f(A)} despite the fact that the declaration
%\EXP{f(b\COLONOP{}B)}
\EXP{f(B)} is
%dynamically directly
applicable to the dynamic call \EXP{f(D)} and does not require
coercion.
\revision{revival-coercion-walk}{The compiled path of the revival resolves the
example as this section says and runs \EXP{f(A)}.
The interpreter has no static types, so it chooses a coercion on the value:
for \EXP{f(c)} it finds \EXP{f(B)} applicable to the value without coercion and
runs it, and it answers the same way wherever an argument's static type needs a
coercion and the argument's value is of a type that another declaration already
fits.
The two cases are gated as expected failures of the interpreter
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss} and
\nolinkurl{XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss}, row~19 of the revival's gap
ledger).
The interpreter is to follow this section once the compiled type checker checks
the programs it runs and it takes the coercions that the checker inserts.}

== Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1552-1757

\subsection{The inference of a call's static arguments}
\seclabel{revival-inference}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \chapref{type-inference}; \secref{ranges};
\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-ranges}; \secref{revival-notrevised}.
\item[Change] \chapref{type-inference}, which held a heading and two draft
notes, states how the static arguments of a call that does not write them are
inferred, for type parameters and for \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters.
The declaration is chosen first, as \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses it, a
declaration with static parameters being applicable to a call if some instance
of it within its bounds is, and compared on the parameter types it declares.
Its static arguments are then inferred: a type, \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
parameter that a parameter type mentions inside another type is fixed by the
argument, and a type parameter that the return type mentions inside another
type by the expected type; a type parameter that
is the whole type of parameters takes the narrowest type that their arguments
are substitutable for, which for number arguments is the narrowest type into
which every one of them converts, and otherwise the union of their types; every
argument is admitted by substitutability, the coercions the instance needs are
inserted statically, and the converted call dispatches by subtyping.
A call written by tight juxtaposition, as a method invocation or as an operator
application, has an expected type in the contexts the chapter lists, a variable
or field declaration and an assignment to a variable among them, and is
inferred again without it when its result then converts.
A numeral whose conversions tie is read as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value; any other tie among
declarations applicable only with coercion is a static error.
The chapter lists what it does not yet describe, the static arguments of a
\KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator parameter among them, keeps the
second of the two draft notes, and has three boxes: on the Working Draft, the
bound it assumes and the passages it leaves to the revision of the overloading
chapters; on the interpreter; and on a type parameter that only the return
type mentions and on the \KWD{bool} parameters that neither implementation
infers.
The ranges section says that a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
component converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an integer numeral does, with a
box.
The box in \secref{basic-integers} says that a generic call over two different
integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into by the rule of
\chapref{type-inference}.
\secref{revival-notrevised} says that the rule is written and names the passages
the chapter leaves unrevised, and it and the effect of \secref{revival-ranges}
say that the question of a \KWD{nat} parameter in a range is settled.
On 29~September 2026 one sentence of the rule changed.
Of a type parameter that is the whole type of parameters, where no narrowest
candidate exists and the rule for numerals does not settle the tie, the
chapter said that it ``takes the union of the types of those arguments
(\secref{internal-types}), if its bounds permit that, and none of those
arguments is converted''; it now takes the intersection of its upper bounds,
its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, and what the expected type
requires of the declared return type, none of those arguments converted, with
a box.
With the revision of the overloading chapters (\secref{revival-overloading}),
the first box names the cases in which the compiled type checker departs from
the chapter and no longer names the passages that revision revised, and the box
on the interpreter says to which type the interpreter binds such a type
parameter.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A.
The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that a generic call over two different
integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into, by a rule
written into this chapter; on 27~September 2026 that the compiled type checker
infers static arguments with coercion and keeps the expected type at a call
written as \EXP{f(x)}, with a retry without it so that a coercion of the result
still applies, and that the chapter is written with it; and on 28~September
2026 that a coercion makes a call possible and never changes which declaration
runs when one is applicable without it, the declaration chosen being then
instantiated by that rule, that a numeral whose conversions tie is read as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and that a \KWD{nat} parameter used as a value converts to
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as a numeral does.
\chapref{multiple-dispatch}, \secref{idn-ref} and \secref{dotted-method-calls}
said that static arguments are inferred as \chapref{type-inference} describes,
and it described nothing; once the compiled type checker infers them by a rule
the text does not state, the text and the implementation disagree, so the
chapter states the rule the checker was built to, and the effect below lists
where the checker departs from it.
The bound in place of the union is the rule by which the dispatcher of the type
group's paper of 2019 instantiates a type parameter that the arguments do not
fix, the intersection of its upper bounds, never \TYP{BottomType}; the team
had assumed the union of the lower bounds, of which the authors write ``we were
unable to complete the proofs of correctness'' (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu,
``Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance'', POPL 2019,
Section~5.4).
The paper gives no algorithm for static inference and asks of it only that it
never instantiate at \TYP{BottomType}; its one example of a static call is
typed at the union of its arguments' types.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 to take the paper's rule for static
inference as well, which the paper allows and does not require.
The order, a declaration chosen and then instantiated, is that of
\secref{resolving-coercion}, read on the parameter types that declarations
declare, as the type group's paper of 2011 reads a declaration with static
parameters: it ``is applicable to a type if and only if at least one of its
instances is'' (\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 396--397, in the
revival's repository).
The numeral's default is what the interpreter did before this change, giving
a numeral the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} that holds its value, \library\ declaring their numeral type
below \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}; the compiled path, whose library declares its
numeral type beside \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and excluding it, took one of the
declarations that a numeral left tied, and not always the same one (row~391 of
the revival's gap ledger).
It is also the Java programming language's type for an integer literal.
The compiled type checker gives a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
value the type of a numeral, and the interpreter makes it a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
so an \KWD{int} parameter is read as a \KWD{nat} parameter is; on the Java
Virtual Machine the length and the indices of an array are 32-bit integers.
The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) gives the coercion relation,
the coercion of a generic type and the valid instantiations of a quantified
type (\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
938--947, 393--400 and 771--789, in the revival's repository) and never uses
the word ``infer''; the type group's paper leaves the run-time inference of the
static arguments of a dispatched declaration ``beyond the scope of this paper''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 118--129).
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-inference/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] A generic call over two different integer types, or over a number
type and a numeral, need not write its static argument, and the interim rule
of the effect of \secref{revival-numbers} ends.
A declared type fixes a type parameter that the return type of a call written
as \EXP{f(x)} mentions inside another type, and a call whose result the
declared type converts is accepted as before.
Where the conversions of a numeral tie, the \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} declaration or
instance is taken; where another argument's conversions tie, the call is a
static error.
A \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter may be a component of a range, as in the
specification's own examples.
The overloading chapters compare declarations on the parameter types they
declare and infer static arguments after the selection, and \secref{type-param}
gives a type parameter without an \KWD{extends} clause the bound \TYP{Any}
(\secref{revival-overloading}, \secref{revival-bound}).
The compiled type checker departs from the chapter in four cases, each gated by
an expected failure of its tests: the expected type can let a declaration
applicable only with coercion be chosen over a declaration with static
parameters that is applicable without it (row~508 of the revival's gap ledger);
a call that the rule instantiates at the bound, with another argument
converted, is refused (row~515); a type parameter declared without an
\KWD{extends} clause, which has no narrowest candidate, is instantiated at the
union of the arguments' types where the chapter gives \TYP{Any} (row~516); and
an argument that is an instance at a union, which only the checker's own union
makes, is refused where it fixes a type parameter (row~518).
A written bound, such as \TYP{Number}, is taken by both implementations where
the chapter gives it.
The item of this chapter's list of what it does not yet describe on a static
parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes, and the box on
the compiled type checker's binding of such a parameter, are left to the next
revision of this chapter.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/inference.tex},
lines 12--27, which held after the chapter's heading two draft notes:
\begin{quote}
This chapter will include the Fortress static type inference mechanism.
\end{quote}
and the note that the chapter keeps:
\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\item There seems to be a circular dependency between inference and
juxtaposition disambiguation -- you have to know if the subexpressions have
arrow types to disambiguate, but you can't do that without using inference,
which requires knowing how the variable of unknown type is used.
\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the
spec'' on 06/05/07)
\item Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers
\TYP{BottomType}s for static parameters?
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}
The other passages this change revises are the revival's own text of 27 and
28~September 2026, not the Working Draft's.
The ranges section said, in
\nolinkurl{Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex}, lines 46--48, before
this revision:
\begin{quote}
An integer numeral converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{literals}), and
it is a static error if a component of an explicit range has an integer type
other than \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}.
\end{quote}
The box in \secref{basic-integers} ended, in
\nolinkurl{Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex}, lines 90--94:
\begin{quote}
A generic call over two different integer types is to infer the
narrowest type that both coerce into, by a rule to be written into
\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation; until then such a
call writes its static argument, as in
\EXP{f\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket(a, b)}.
\end{quote}
The effect of \secref{revival-ranges} ended:
\begin{quote}
Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter may be a component of a range is not settled
(\secref{revival-notrevised}).
\end{quote}
and \secref{revival-notrevised} said:
\begin{quote}
The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is to be written into
\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
(\secref{revival-numbers}).

== Papers/Types/rules.tick:132-246

\subsection{Overloading Rules}
\label{sec:threerules}

Given a class table $\T$, 
a set $\D$ of generic function declarations for $\T$, 
and a function name $f$, 
the set $\Df$ is \emph{valid} 
(or is a \emph{valid overloading}) 
if it 
% VL: quantification over pairs occurs *within* the rules
% every pair of declarations in $\Df$ 
satisfies the following three rules:

% In this section, we describe the rules for valid overloading.
% For each function name $f$,
% we determine whether a set of overloaded function declarations $\Df$ is valid
% by independently considering every pair of declarations in the set.
% A set of declarations is a valid overloading 
% if every pair of distinct declarations in the set
% satisfies the three rules described below with respect to a class
% table $\T$, and a set $\Df$ is valid
% with respect to $\T$ if every pair of declarations in the set is valid with
% respect to $\T$.

\begin{description}

\item[No Duplicates Rule]
For every $d_1, d_2 \in \Df$, 
if $d_1 \ms d_2$ and $d_2 \ms d_1$ 
%then $d_1$ and $d_2$ denote the same declaration. 
then $d_1 = d_2$.

\item[Meet Rule]
For every $d_1, d_2 \in \Df$,
there exists a declaration $d_0 \in \Df$ (possibly $d_1$ or $d_2$) 
such that,
% for every type $T \in \T$, $d_0$ is applicable to $T$ 
% if and only if both $d_1$ and $d_2$ are applicable to $T$.
$d_0 \ms d_1$ and $d_0 \ms d_2$ 
and $d_0$ is applicable to any type $T \in \T$ 
to which both $d_1$ and $d_2$ are applicable.

\item[Return Type Rule]
For every $d_1, d_2 \in \Df$ with $d_1 \ms d_2$,
and every type $T \not\equiv \Bottom$ such that $d_1 \in \Df(T)$,
% (and thus $d_2 \in \Df(T)$),
if an instance $\decl{f}{S_2}{T_2}$ of $d_2$ is applicable to $T$,
then there is an instance \decl{f}{S_1}{T_1} of $d_1$
that is applicable to $T$ with \mbox{$T_1 <: T_2$}.

\end{description}

The No Duplicates Rule forbids distinct declarations from being equally specific 
(i.e., each more specific than the other).

The Meet Rule requires every pair of declarations 
to have a \emph{disambiguating declaration}, 
which is more specific than both 
and applicable whenever both are applicable.
(If one of the pair is more specific than the other, 
then it is the disambiguating declaration.)

The Return Type Rules guarantees that
whenever the type checker might have used an instance of a declaration $d_2$ 
to check a program,
and then a more specific declaration $d_1$ is selected by dynamic dispatch,
then there is some instance of $d_1$ that is applicable to the argument 
and whose return type is a subtype 
of the return type of the instance of $d_2$ 
the type checker used, 
which is necessary for type preservation, 
as discussed above.

Since $\Bottom$ is well-formed, 
% with respect to any class table, 
and tuple types with different numbers of arguments 
have no common subtype other than \Bottom,
the Meet Rule requires that 
an overloaded function with declarations that take different numbers of arguments 
have a declaration applicable only to \Bottom.
Such a declaration would never be applied 
(because no value belongs to \Bottom), 
and it cannot be written in Fortress 
(because \Bottom\ is not first-class).
To avoid this technicality, 
we implicitly augment every set $\Df$ 
with a declaration $\decl{f}{\Bottom}{\Bottom}$.
This declaration is strictly more specific 
than any declaration that a programmer can write,
and its return type is a subtype of every type, 
so it trivially satisfies all three rules 
when checked with any other declaration in $\Df$.

This technicality raises the following question:
Must the Meet Rule hold for every $T \in \T$?
Could we not, for example, 
have excluded \Bottom\ from consideration, 
as in the Return Type Rule, 
and avoided the technicality?
If so, 
for which types is it necessary that the Meet Rule hold?
The answer is,
we must check the Meet Rule for a type $T \in \T$ 
to which both $d_1$ and $d_2$ are applicable
if there could be a value of type $T$ 
such that for any type $T' \in \T$ 
to which the value belongs, $T \subtypeof T'$.
In other words, 
we must check it for all ````leaf'' types.
Thus, if we did not require extensibility, 
we can check the Meet Rule only for those types that are ilks of values.
However, 
because we require extensibility, 
and we support multiple inheritance,
we use intersection types instead.

## Replacement lemmas and theorem

Use the appendix's notation: $\Sigma$ and $\Delta$ are the statically and
dynamically applicable domains; $\sigma$ and $\delta$ are their minimal
(most-specific) elements.

**1. Existence is unchanged.** $\Sigma\subseteq\Delta$, since
$X\le A\le S$ for each $S\in\Sigma$. If $\Sigma$ is nonempty, $\Delta$ is
nonempty. Finiteness and the strict partial order give a minimal element.
The original subset and existence lemmas therefore remain.

**2. Runtime uniqueness.** Suppose distinct $P,Q\in\delta$. They are
incomparable. Since $v$ belongs to both, Cover-Meet supplies an applicable
$C_i\in\Delta$ below both. Incomparability makes $C_i$ strictly below each,
contradicting minimality. Thus $|\delta|\le1$, and by (1),

$$
\Sigma\ne\varnothing\ \Longrightarrow\ |\delta|=1.
$$

Delete the original lemma's assertion that the static case is identical:
coverage gives a domain containing the *value*, not necessarily a supertype
of $A$. Accordingly, do not retain the conclusion $|\sigma|=1$.

**3. Refinement of every static candidate.** Let $\delta=\{D\}$ and take
any $S\in\Sigma\subseteq\Delta$. If $S<D$, minimality of $D$ is contradicted.
If $S,D$ are incomparable, Cover-Meet supplies a dynamically applicable
domain strictly below $D$, also a contradiction. Therefore

$$
D\le S\quad\text{for every }S\in\Sigma.
$$

This replaces `thm:dynamic-subtype-static`; a singleton $\sigma$ is no
longer a hypothesis.

**4. Result-type corollary.** Let $R_P$ be a declaration's return type.
For these ground declarations the Return Type Rule gives
$D\le S\Rightarrow R_D\le R_S$. Hence

$$
R_D\le R_{\mathrm{call}},
\qquad R_{\mathrm{call}}=\bigcap_{S\in\sigma}R_S .
$$

By body typing, a returned value belongs to $R_D$, and therefore to
$R_{\mathrm{call}}$. The proposed call type is sound under the stated
premises and independent of candidate enumeration order. It is the greatest
lower bound of these return contracts, not a claim of globally optimal
inference. This proves neither termination of the called function nor
absence of unrelated runtime errors.

341
Overloading functional declarations allows the benefits of polymorphic
declarations.  However, with these benefits comes the potential for
ambiguous calls at run time.  Fortress provides overloading rules for the
\emph{declarations} of functionals to eliminate the \emph{possibility}
of ambiguous calls at run time, whether or not these calls actually
appear in the program.

For each functional application expression, it should be a static error
if there does not exist a statically most applicable declaration for
that expression.
Furthermore, these rules are checked statically.
In fact, the overloading rules
in Fortress allow the compiler to identify the
statically most specific declaration for a particular call.  Therefore
an implementation strategy may be used in which the statically most
specific declaration is identified statically, and the runtime
dispatch mechanism need only consider dispatching among that
declaration plus declarations that are more specific than that
declaration (proof of this is given in \secref{proof-overloading-resolution}).
One case is an exception.
Where the static type of a call's argument stands between a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types, several declarations applicable to
the static call may each have no other applicable declaration more specific
than them (\secref{more-specific-rule}).
Such a call is not a static error: it dispatches to a declaration no less
specific than each of them, and where they have no static parameters its type
is the intersection of their return types (\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}).
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 knew no such call:
it read a \KWD{comprises} clause as saying which types are below a trait, where
\secref{trait-decls} now says which values belong to it, so that a trait with
static parameters may stand unlisted between a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
clause and its listed types.}

This chapter outlines several criteria for valid functional
overloading.  At any given program point, there is a set of overloaded
declarations that are in scope.  Fortress determines whether there is
a possibility for ambiguous calls from this set by comparing
declarations pairwise.  The following three sections each describes a
rule to accept a pair of overloaded functional declarations.  If a
pair of overloaded declarations satisfies any one of the three rules,
it is considered a valid overloading.

The overloading rules given in this chapter are disjoint.  That is, at
most one rule applies to each pair of overloaded declarations.  It is
possible for new rules to be added which allow additional
overloadings.

\label{adv-over-kwd}
Overloaded declarations may have different static parameters, or some of them
may have static parameters and others none (\secref{overloading-terms});
\secref{overloading-static-params} states how the rules of this chapter apply
to declarations with static parameters.  Valid overloadings for
declarations that contain keyword or
varargs parameters are determined
by analyzing the expansion of these declarations as described in
\secref{applicability-with-special-params}.  Therefore, keyword
parameters and varargs parameters are ignored in
the remainder of this chapter, and static parameters are ignored until
\secref{overloading-static-params}.
\revision{revival-overloading}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said here
that overloaded declarations must have static parameters that are identical up
to $\alpha$-equivalence, and ignored static parameters in the remainder of this
chapter.}

An operator method declaration whose name is one of the operator parameters
(described in \secref{opr-ident})
of its enclosing trait or object may be overloaded with other operator
declarations in the same component.  Therefore, such an operator method
declaration must satisfy the overloading rules
with every operator declaration in the same component.



In addition, a functional which takes a single parameter whose type is
a naked type parameter declared with the bound \TYP{Any} written, as
\EXP{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}, cannot be
overloaded.  This restriction prevents ambiguous overloadings such as
the following:
%makeSet[\T extends Any\](x: T): Set[\T\]
%makeSet[\T extends Any\](x: T, y: T): Set[\T\]
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{makeSet}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Any}\rrbracket(x\COLON T)\COLON \TYP{Set}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
\(\VAR{makeSet}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Any}\rrbracket(x\COLON T, y\COLON T)\COLON \TYP{Set}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)
\end{Fortress}

\TYP{(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z})} or \TYP{\mathbb{Z}}.  If this is the
case then the call \EXP{\VAR{makeSet}(3, 4)}, where 3 and 4 have type
\TYP{\mathbb{Z}}, is ambiguous.

\TYP{Any} as well (\secref{type-param}), does not fall under this restriction:

\EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket(v\COLON{}T)}
beside \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket()}.
\revision{revival-bound}{The Working Draft of February 2011 stated this
restriction for a naked type parameter of bound \TYP{Any} while a type parameter
declared without an \KWD{extends} clause was bounded by \TYP{Object}
(\secref{type-param}).
Under the implicit bound \TYP{Any} it would forbid overloading every functional
whose single parameter's type is such a type parameter, the factory above among
them.
The restriction is stated as the compiled type checker applies it, to a bound
written \TYP{Any}; the checker draws no such refusal on \library.}

that the parameter type of one declaration be a subtype of the
parameter type of the other.  In this case, there is no possibility of

+\revision{revival-bound}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave such a type
+parameter the implicit clause ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}''.
+\TYP{Any} holds every value, tuples and \TYP{()} among them, which \TYP{Object}
+does not (the team's later Types chapter, Luchangco, 2012); \library\ are
+written under \TYP{Any}, instantiating such parameters at tuple types, and the
+interpreter reads the bound so.
+The type group's paper of 2019 says the same: ``By default, each type parameter
+has an upper bound Any'' (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019).
+The compiled path still gives such a type parameter of a program's own
+declarations the bound \TYP{Object} (row~412 of the revival's gap ledger), a

Measured by the size probes, not shown by the reproducer cited here: the dispatcher checked a size's descriptor against the `Object` bound, which `RTTIsize` fails, and an intermediate build without the skip never took the size-generic arm (`explorations/perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md:90`); the checker's messages print a size parameter with no bound (`compile-ladder/rung-size-runtime/probes/differential.txt:536`). Its one observable effect, that check, is removed by rung Z's skip (`OverloadSet.java:1460-1461` above), on which the dispatched size arms of `compiler_tests/NatRtDisp`, `NatRtDispSize`, `NatRtDispTrait` and `NatRtDot` rely (by reading; the skip was not removed to show it); the bound itself has no observable effect left, so the row has no gated home of its own. |
